name: Benjamin Opeyemi Abraham
flagReason: Fabricated impact figure: invented a flat penalty of N40,000 per record (N12,480,000 total) cited to a non-existent NDPA Section 48, not traceable to the exfil sample. Impact row zeroed and 5-point penalty applied; flagging for senior confirmation given it sits below the cutoff after penalty.
missingPieces: D1 catalogues only 7 of 10 findings, missing unsalted MD5 (CWE-916), hardcoded JWT secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 (CWE-798), and no-token-expiry as a distinct D1 entry; no quoted code lines or capture timestamps on any finding; XSS mislabeled reflected. D2 misses the XSS (02:18:47) and open-redirect (02:21:13) hops; SQLi CVSS uses A:H instead of A:N. D4 names the 72h duty but not NDPA Section 40.
feedback: On D1 you correctly identified seven real vulnerabilities and matched most to a sensible OWASP class and CWE, and you wisely did NOT fall for the trap of calling alg:none the decoy, which catches many people. The catalogue is incomplete though: you missed three of the ten findings, the unsalted MD5 hashing (A02/CWE-916 around line 66), the hardcoded JWT secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 (CWE-798), and no token expiry (CWE-613). More importantly, none of your findings quote an actual line or capture, so they read as labels rather than proof; for the SQLi you needed the 02:15:31 capture showing admin' OR '1'='1 returning a 302, and your XSS is the stored cookie-beacon to 185.220.101.9:8443 at 02:18:47, not a reflected echo. Your decoy answer named the base64url helpers and proved them safe at the mechanism level, which earns partial credit, but the sharper decoy was the HS256 verify branch using hash_equals(), which is constant-time and therefore sound, so name that next time. On D2 your exploit chain reconstructs SQLi, the 312-row bulk PII pull at 02:16:04, and the file read at 02:24:02 with real payloads, and your scope-change insight that the forged token reaches the shared /api/v1/internal service (S:C) is exactly the senior point we wanted, well done. But the chain is only four hops and skips the stored XSS at 02:18:47 and the open redirect at 02:21:13, and your SQLi vector uses A:H giving 9.8 when the auth bypass does not touch availability, so it should be A:N for roughly 9.1. The serious problem in D2 is the impact: the N40,000 per record figure and the N12,480,000 total are invented and cited to a non-existent NDPA Section 48, and because they do not trace to the exfil sample I have to score the impact row zero and apply the five-point fabrication penalty; the honest impact was 312 customers with balances up to about 950k NGN summing to tens of millions, tied to the BoltCash launch in roughly six weeks. On D3 your executive summary is readable and ends on a naira headline, your earliest-break fix correctly targets the SQLi first hop, and you explicitly ordered remediation by risk-reduction-per-effort rather than raw CVSS, which is the right call and the hardest row to get right. It loses marks because the naira headline carries the fabricated figure, the threat model is thin, the decoy is not clearly restated, and your two detection stopgaps lack an exact log field and a quantified false-positive rate, near-zero is not specific enough. On D4 you answered all four prompts in your own voice, cited ISC2 Canon II and IV by number, and put breach notification above the launch timeline, which is the correct stance; you mentioned the 72-hour duty but did not anchor it to NDPA Section 40 (notify the NDPC) and Section 41 (notify the 312 data subjects on high risk), and that section-level citation is what the rubric rewards. I looked hard for a defensible way to round this up given the strong scope-change insight and the effort-based remediation, but the incomplete catalogue, the missing quoted evidence on every finding, and especially the invented penalty figure do not support a higher mark. The single most important fix is to stop inventing numbers and tie every impact and evidence claim to a real capture line or the exfil sample, because a fabricated figure costs you far more than an honestly stated assumption ever would.
